idiom_name: function type as the strategy (interface or record of strategies for named/typed variants)
implementation_notes: A strategy in TypeScript is a function type: type PricingStrategy = (qty: number) => number is the whole contract, and the context holds it as a field or constructor parameter, which is what Array.prototype.sort's compare function does in the language itself. Two refinements carry their weight: a Record keyed by a literal union (Record<'retail' | 'bulk', PricingStrategy>) gives a checked, exhaustively-listed registry for configuration-driven selection, and an interface (or class implementing it) is worth it when the strategy has state, exposes several operations, or must be mocked by name. When the variants differ mainly in their data rather than their behaviour, prefer a discriminated union plus a dispatch function over one class per variant.
pitfalls: Types are erased at run time: a strategy looked up with a widened string key (strategies[key]) compiles to undefined and fails at the call, so keep the key a literal union and validate external input at the boundary.
Passing a class method as a strategy loses this; the call throws or reads undefined fields - bind it (obj.method.bind(obj)) or use an arrow-function property.

Structural typing accepts any function with a compatible signature, so a mis-wired but type-compatible strategy passes the compiler; the record-of-strategies form keeps each key tied to its intended implementation.
